sensitivities.case: Baseline: Census as published for Milwaukee
sensitivities.description: Baseline over 2027-2031 without the Milwaukee apartment adjustment (the parking addition does not change).

Baseline over 2027-2031 from a model trained on places with no parking reform nationwide, 0.97 times the same-pace baseline. In held-out tests no model beat same pace: on single cities same pace is as good as any, and on state totals the tree models only match same pace with a national level adjustment. Same pace ran 17-23% low in 2020-2025. The parking addition does not change.

Baseline over 2027-2031 if 2020-2025's strength continues: 134,323 (random forest, scikit-learn; owner 2026-11-02: no dependency on the removed econml package; its honest forest gave a similar figure), and up to {w['M0L same pace x level']:,.0f} if every place keeps 2020-2025's full level over its earlier pace. In Wisconsin's own 2021-2025 back-test, same pace came in at 0.77 of actual, the forests at 0.95 and the full-level version at 1.01. The parking addition does not change (docs/parking/BASELINE_MODELS_RESULTS.md).

trace.text: Census building permits by municipality and building size, 2023–2025 average; Milwaukee's apartments estimated from the city's property file.

From 74 US repeal places compared with similar places: their measured average (-1.15 permits per 1,000 homes per year) plus the low end of the spread of 20,000 placebo studies of cities that never repealed, applied to Wisconsin's eligible homes without a floor at zero.
The same measured average plus the high end of the placebo spread (owner choice; the resampling high end is a sensitivity).

The measured average of the 74 repeal places against similar places, without a floor at zero; pulled down mostly by Austin, Minneapolis and San Francisco. Held-out repeal places are predicted best by no effect.

The evidence centres near zero (weighted by homes slightly below, each place equal slightly above). The low end is the measured average and may be below zero; no line is cut off at zero without evidence (owner rule).

Before repeal, repeal places did not move in step with their comparison places (a gap of about 2 permits per 1,000 homes a year over the 5 years before). Allowing for that, the range of the measured average is about −5.6 to +3.5 permits per 1,000 homes a year, wider than −3.5 to +1.4 (owner, 2026-11-03).
A simulation with fake repeals found these 90% ranges cover the truth about 84% of the time, so the true range is about a sixth wider (owner, 2026-11-03).

Each scenario uses its own measured timing (owner, 2026-11-10). For parking the measured timing is flat: year 1 after repeal can't be told apart from years 2–3 (36 places; every year's range includes 0), and the by-year test on places with 5+ years after repeal found no build-up or fade (Test 49). So the same yearly rate applies in every year 2027–2031.

trace.part: Years 4–5 and evidence carrying over to Wisconsin
trace.text: The effect was measured over years 1–3 in other places (and up to 9 years for 13 places, with no clear trend); it is held flat for 2030–2031 and applied in Wisconsin.

Spread in proportion to existing homes; places that already have no minimums for housing, or removed them with conditions, get none. Madison and Milwaukee, which removed them only in some districts, get the full rate, which may overstate their share.
